summary: Private equity is getting easier for Indian investors to reach. Whether that means better opportunities or just different and harder-to-see risks is the actual question. This one goes through how professional private-equity managers pick companies, judge founders, do due diligence, set valuations and, most importantly, plan the exit before they invest. Because in private markets, finding a good company is only part of the job. Someone has to buy it from you.

seo.title: Unlisted Shares & Pre-IPO: What Investors Get Wrong
seo.description: Unlisted shares, pre-IPO and AIFs: how private equity managers pick, value and exit, and the liquidity and valuation risks investors miss.

takeaways.text: In private markets the exit is the hard part. A great company you cannot sell is not a great investment.
Pre-IPO attracts people with the promise of extraordinary returns, and the three risks they tend to skip are liquidity, valuation and information asymmetry.
The valuation you enter at decides most of your outcome, and in unlisted markets the information behind that valuation is far thinner than in listed ones.
Category I, II and III AIFs are different things. Knowing which one you are being sold, and where private equity and private credit sit inside them, is the starting point.
If an IPO is delayed or never arrives, pre-IPO investors can be stuck for years, which is why continuation funds exist at all.

fork.decision: You want exposure to unlisted companies. Buy the shares yourself, or go through a fund?

points.text: You keep the whole return instead of sharing it with a manager and a fee structure.
The access that used to be institutional is genuinely opening up to individual investors.
You choose the specific company rather than inheriting someone else's portfolio.
Professional managers do due diligence that includes speaking to the company's actual customers, which you cannot replicate.
They plan the exit before they invest, and exit is where private equity mostly goes wrong.
A fund diversifies across companies, so one delayed IPO does not take your whole allocation with it.

fork.pick: If you cannot answer who will buy this from you and at what valuation you are entering, you are not investing in a company, you are hoping for a listing. That research is a full-time job, which is the argument for paying someone whose full-time job it is.
